subject: Art & Design
title: Brutalism: Concrete as Art
description: A quick, practical guide to Brutalism: Concrete as Art.

hook.text: Massive, raw concrete slabs. No ornamentation. Brutalist buildings are loved and hated in equal measure.

buildup.text: Brutalism (1950s–70s) used exposed concrete ('béton brut') and bold geometric forms. It was deliberately unrefined.

discovery.text: Born from post-war rebuilding, Brutalism offered honest, affordable structures for public housing and civic buildings.

twist.text: Most people found Brutalist buildings cold and oppressive. Many were demolished. Now they're being listed as heritage.

climax.text: The Barbican in London and Habitat 67 in Montreal are now celebrated icons of the movement.

punchline.text: Brutalism asked: can raw honesty be beautiful? The debate rages on.

quiz.question: Where does the term 'Brutalism' come from?
options: From 'béton brut' — the French term for raw concrete
From architect Bruno Brutali who founded the movement

details.summary: Brutalism (1950s-1970s) celebrated raw concrete (béton brut) left unfinished as both structure and surface. Massive geometric forms, repetitive patterns, and bold sculptural compositions characterized buildings like the Barbican in London and Habitat 67 in Montreal.
details.whyItMatters: Brutalism is architecture's most divisive style — loved for its honesty and sculptural power, hated for its cold, imposing presence.
takeaways: Raw concrete served as both structure and decorative surface
Massive geometric forms and bold compositions define the style
Brutalism remains architecture's most polarizing movement

faq.question: Why is it called Brutalism?
faq.answer: From the French 'béton brut' meaning raw concrete — not from 'brutal.' The name refers to the honest expression of concrete as a building material without finishes or cladding. The unfortunate English association with brutality has unfairly colored public perception.

faq.question: Why do many people dislike Brutalist buildings?
faq.answer: Raw concrete weathers poorly in damp climates, staining and cracking. Many Brutalist housing projects were poorly maintained and associated with social problems. The massive scale can feel oppressive. However, well-maintained examples like the Barbican are now highly desirable.
